Full Length Article 
Importance of digester’s headspace geometry for the efficient H2S removal 
through microaeration; experimental and simulation study 
Mark´eta Andreides *, Lucie Pokorn´a-Krayzelov´a , Jan Bart´aˇcek 
Department of Water Technology and Environmental Engineering, University of Chemistry and Technology Prague, Technick´a 5, 166 28 Prague 6, Czech Republic   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
CFD model 
Desulfurization of biogas 
Headspace geometry 
Microaeration 
A B S T R A C T   
Microaeration for biogas desulfurization occurs mainly in the headspace of anaerobic digesters where the biofilm 
growth is mainly reported; however, no study has been focused on the effect of headspace geometry on 
microaeration performance. This research evaluates the effect of headspace geometry on biogas flow, subsequent 
biofilm growth, and the effect of these parameters on microaeration efficiency. This effect was studied in an 
anaerobic digester with three different headspace configurations. Also, the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) 
model explained the experimental results. The CFD model developed described the biogas flow in all headspace 
configurations. It was proven that the modifications of headspace geometry altered biogas flow and avoided 
biofilm growth on the reactor walls leading to the reactor’s protection from the adverse effects of biofilm growth. 
The mathematical model developed in this work can help design microaerobic digesters or find the best way to 
implement microaeration into the digesters already built.   
1. Introduction 
Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is an inevitable product of the anaerobic 
treatment of sulfur-rich substrates [1]. Sulfur-rich substrates are, e.g. 
sludges from urban wastewater treatment plants (WWTP), agricultural 
resources, or animal waste. The amount of total sulfur in g/kg (sulfur/ 
total solids) in these substrates is, e.g. 4.5 (primary sludge), 8.6 (acti­
vated sludge), 4.0 (camelina crops), 8.0 (pig slurry) [2]. Poisonous H2S 
causes concrete and steel corrosion in anaerobic digesters leading to the 
shortening of the technology’s lifetime. Also, H2S in biogas acidifies 
engine oil in cogeneration units and can disqualify biogas from 
upgrading to biomethane [3]. Therefore, it is of great importance to 
remove H2S from biogas before its further use. 
Several methods for biogas desulfurization are already used in in­
dustry, including, e.g. biotrickling filters, biofilters, or bioscrubbers. 
Detailed information and comparison of these methods can be found in 
Andreides et al. [4]. In the past decade, microaeration, a bio-based 
method, has garnered significant attention owing to its high efficiency 
and relative simplicity [5]. Despite its widespread application in full- 
scale installations, the theoretical description of this technique funda­
mental bases have not been adequately elucidated. To address this gap, 
the present study utilizes mathematical modeling to enhance our current 
understanding of its fundamental principles. 
In microaeration, H2S is biologically oxidized to harmless elemental 
sulfur by sulfide oxidizing bacteria (SOB). The growth of SOB is sup­
ported by controlled dosing of air or oxygen into the anaerobic digesters 
[6]. Next to desulfurization, dosing of limited air/oxygen into the liquid 
phase enhances the hydrolysis of organic material and increases 
methane production [7]. ORP-controlled based oxygenation can keep 
the level of sulfide concentration in the liquid phase [8]. The impact of 
several factors on microaeration efficiency has been documented, 
including air dose (e.g. Díaz et al. [9], biogas residence time in the 
headspace [10], pH in the liquid phase (e.g. Krayzelova et al. [11], and 
the position of oxygen dosing point (e.g. Díaz et al. [12]. The results vary 
throughout the literature with no apparent explanation. There is a 
presumption that the microaeration strategy decision could be based on 
the headspace geometry and position of the oxygen dosing point. 
It was proven that regardless of whether oxygen is dosed into the 
liquid or gas phase, desulfurization occurs mainly in the digester’s 
headspace[13]. When there is no headspace in the digester, desulfur­
ization does not take place since SOB are usually present in the biofilm 
covering the walls of the headspace where H2S and oxygen is available 
[3,12]. When oxygen is provided into the liquid, microaeration usually 
is not efficient enough, since oxygen is used for oxidation of organic 
compounds and other processes. The increase in oxygen supply, how­
ever, could disrupt the anaerobic conditions. I.e., providing sufficient

surface area for the growth of SOB biofilm is vital for assuring efficient 
removal of H2S from biogas. This biofilm can, however, cause clogging 
of biogas pipes and destruction of the structural materials [3,5,13]. 
According to our best knowledge, no clear protection strategy against 
harmful biofilm effects is defined in the literature. 
Headspace geometry can affect the pattern of biogas flow and the 
efficiency of microaeration. Also, it can direct biofilm growth to loca­
tions where harmful effects will be mitigated. However, the effect of the 
headspace geometry on biogas and/or oxygen flow and subsequent 
biofilm growth and microaeration efficiency has not been evaluated yet. 
Moreover, headspace geometry is usually not even mentioned in the 
research papers dealing with microaeration efficiency. Nevertheless, 
there is an assumption that if the biofilm growth were transferred from 
the reactor walls to a properly designed “sacrificial object”, the reactor 
walls would remain protected, thereby extending the technology’s 
lifespan. 
In a lab-scale digester with variable headspace geometry, we studied 
the effect of headspace geometry on biogas and oxygen flow, biofilm 
growth, and microaeration efficiency. The experimental results from 
three tested headspace configurations were explained using a 3D 
computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model developed in COMSOL 
Multiphysics (COMSOL, Sweden). Our results show that adding properly 
designed baffles into the headspace can shift the biofilm growth to the 
baffles, and the walls of the digester can be protected. The model can be 
easily adjusted to other reactors only by modifying the geometry of its 
headspace. Therefore, the model can be a tool for ideal headspace design 
or evaluating the geometry effect on gas flow in existing reactors. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Experimental study 
2.1.1. Experimental setup 
Two laboratory semi-continuous anaerobic digesters were built to 
study gas flow and sulfur-driven biofilm growth in the digester’s head­
space (Fig. 1). First digester with empty headspace served as control, 
and the second digester with variable geometry of the headspace was the 
tested digester (see Section 2.1.3). Both digesters were operated for 360 
days (70 days of reaching steady state, 270 days of experiments) at the 
temperature of 44 ◦C. The chosen temperature was intended to maintain 
the conditions of the original inoculum. Both digesters were operated 
under microaerobic conditions, and with operational cycles. One oper­
ational cycle consisted of 50 min settling, 250 min stirring, and 2 min 
feeding. An artificial substrate: cheese whey solution (40 g/L) with the 
addition of K2SO4 (1.8 g/L) was used to increase the amount of H2S in 
the biogas. The artificial substrate provided consistent conditions for all 
ongoing experiments, thus excluding any influence on the results due to 
variations in the composition of the dosed substrate. During the feeding 
time, the substrate was pumped into the bottom part of the reactor. 
Simultaneously, the supernatant from the top level of the liquid phase 
was pumped out from the reactor to keep the volume of the liquid phase 
constant. Both digesters had a total volume of 20 L with liquid and 
headspace volumes of 13 L and 7 L, respectively and were inoculated 
with anaerobic sludge from a mesophilic (44 ◦C) anaerobic digester 
(ˇCesk´a Lípa, Czech Republic). Air is commonly used for microaeration 
purposes due to its simplicity and safety. However, air carries nitrogen 
contamination in the form of biogas, leading to the production of NOx 
during biogas combustion in a cogeneration unit (Rosenberg, personal 
communication, 30th May 2023), which is an undesirable air pollutant. 
Moreover, for our research, pure oxygen was advantageous, as it 
allowed us to dose oxygen more accurately and to quickly detect reactor 
contamination by air when measuring higher concentrations of N2 in the 
biogas, therefore, pure oxygen was used for microaeration. Oxygen was 
dosed continuously into the headspace of both reactors (4 mL h−1) using 
a mass flow controller (Bronkhorst High-Tech B.V., Netherlands). A 
constant oxygen supply in this amount was chosen based on the need to 
monitor residual H2S concentrations to assess the microaeration per­
formance. Complete oxidation would not be desirable in this research. 
2.1.2. Analytical methods 
H2S concentration in biogas was measured every 20 min by an online 
H2S sensor (H2S/SP-10000, Membrapor, Switzerland) equipped with an 
autosampler. The biogas production was measured by gas flow meter 
MilliGascounters (Dr.-Ing. RITTER Apparatebau GmbH & Co. KG, Ger­
many) and was logged every 5 min. H2S concentration, temperature, and 
biogas production measurement were controlled by an in-house pro­
gram developed using LabVIEW 2012 software running on a Compac­
tRIO system (National Instruments, US). 
Chemical oxygen demand, total suspended solids and volatile sus­
pended solids in liquid were measured twice a week according to the 
standard methods [14]. A gas chromatograph (GC 2010, Shimadzu, 
Japan) was used to measure volatile fatty acids in liquid. Samples 
preparation and the GC conditions set-up were done according to 
Andreides et al., 2021 [15]:  
– Samples were centrifuged (13 000 rpm, 14 926 g, for 10 min)

The biogas and air composition in the reactors was measured twice a

– A stainless steel Hayesep D packed column (80/100) for biogas

– The initial temperature of 150 ◦C, the detector temperature of

– Helium was used as the carrier gas.  
– The analysis time for biogas and air detection was 3 and 6 min, 
respectively. 
2.1.3. Experiments with variable headspace geometry 
In the test digester, the cylindrical baffles (Fig. 2) were added to the 
digester to study the difference between biofilm growth positions in 
different headspace configurations. The baffles consisted of three 
concentric cylinders from laminated glass with 10, 15, and 20 cm di­
ameters. The height of the cylinders was 6 cm. The diameter and height 
of the headspace were 24 cm and 10 cm, respectively. The oxygen inlet 
was placed on the digester’s wall 3.5 cm under the ceiling. The cylin­
drical baffles supported biofilm growth and disrupted biogas flow, 
leading to the change of the dominant position of bacterial growth. The 
control digester’s headspace was kept empty to imitate the usual con­
ditions at the digesters. 
The experiments were designed as follows: 
Experiment 1: The headspace of both digesters (control and tested) 
was empty (no added cylinders). 
Experiment 2: The headspace of the control digester was empty; the 
headspace of the tested digester had cylinders. The cylinders were 
suspended 3 cm above the liquid phase surface. Between the ceiling 
and cylinders was a small 1 cm gap. 
Experiment 3: The headspace of the control digester was empty; the 
headspace of the tested digester had cylinders. The cylinders were in 
close contact with the liquid phase. 
Before each experiment, the cylinders were immersed in the liquid 
phase of the reactor (anaerobic sludge) for one day to inoculate their 
surface by seeding bacteria. In all experiments, the biofilm had a growth 
period of at least 90 days. The experiment was terminated when no other 
biofilm shape and quality changes were visually observed. After each 
experiment, the biofilm was completely removed from the walls and 
cylinders. 
2.2. Mathematical simulations 
Software COMSOL Multiphysics with CFD module was used to study 
biogas flow in digesters. Only the headspace geometry was considered in 
the simulation to simplify the model. Based on the calculation of the 
Reynolds number at the reactor outlet, laminar biogas flow in the 
headspace was considered. The Mixture model/Laminar flow was used 
as a second physics to track the oxygen concentration in the modelled 
mixture (biogas/oxygen). Oxygen was modelled here as another phase 
with particle size taken as a diameter of oxygen molecule (0.36 nm). The 
gravity effect was modelled as well. Oxygen flux was set according to the 
actual dose set on the mass flow meter in the laboratory setup. 
In the model, the following assumptions and calculations were taken 
into account:  
– The liquid surface cone was considered negligible in headspace 
geometry.  
– The surface rotation speed was derived according to the rotation 
cone’s size. The calculated rotation speed of the liquid surface was 
52.7 RPM (0.83067 s−1), corresponding to 96 % of the stirrer speed 
(55 RPM).  
– When the cylinders are in contact with liquid, the speed of the liquid 
surface rotation is not changed. 
The experimentally measured biogas flow was considered to calcu­
late the speed of the biogas coming from the liquid, and angular speed 
was calculated according to Eq. (1).

In the model, the 3D geometry of the reactor was built. As modelled 
gases, biogas and oxygen were used. Table 1 describes the properties of 
the gases related to the temperature of 44 ◦C. 
The model was calculated with several meshes to ensure that results 
are not dependent on the mesh configuration. Ultimately, the mesh was 
set as automatic since no dependency was determined. The number of 
elements in the mesh was 785,220, with a maximum element size of 2.6 
cm. The law of conservation of matter was also checked in the model. 
2.3. Overall digesters performance and desulfurization efficiency 
Both reactors were operated stably for 360 days. The values of pH 
and temperature were kept stable at 7.2–7.4 and 44 ◦C, respectively. 
Biogas composition was stable in both digesters (control and tested) for 
the whole operation period. After moisture content correction, biogas’s 
average composition was 0.2 vol% of O2, 60.0 vol% of CH4, and 39.8 vol 
% of CO2. Since the artificial substrate was used, the biogas composition 
was stable and the production was stably around 1200 mL per cycle. 
During the microaeration of the reactors, the H2S concentration 
fluctuated between 10 and a maximum of 160 ppm due to the discon­
tinuous operation (50 min settling, 250 min stirring, 2 min feeding) 
(Fig. 3). The concentration of H2S was intentionally kept at measurable 
levels to allow evaluation of the differences in microaeration efficiency. 
Nevertheless, the efficiency of microaeration remained above 97 % in all 
experiments. The H2S peak period was observed at the beginning of each 
cycle. This phenomenon is caused by the stirring start and rapid release 
of H2S from the liquid. SOB are not able to oxidize it immediately. 
Throughout the experiments, neither the shape of the curve nor the ef­
ficiency of microaeration changed. A detailed study of the influence of 
the stirring intensity on H2S concentration is provided in Andreides et al. 
[3]. 
In Azizi et al. [17], one of the missing pieces of information about 
microaeration in literature is the time required to initiate complete 
desulfurization in the reactor. As written above, the biofilm was 
removed entirely from the reactor after every experiment. When there 
was no aeration, the H2S concentration was around 6000 ppm. After the 
start of aeration, the concentration of H2S dropped within one week, 
even though the biofilm was visibly growing for at least 60 days 
following the start of the oxygen dose. I.e., the biofilm area did not

2.4. Biofilm growth in different reactors configurations 
During the experiment with empty headspace (Experiment 2), the 
biofilm covered the entire digester wall, including the ceiling (Fig. 4A). 
Such a phenomenon is usually visible in full-scale applications. 
When the cylinders had no connection with the liquid phase 
(Experiment 2), biofilm covered the digester’s walls up to 3 cm from the 
liquid surface (Fig. 4B). There was no biofilm between the wall and the 
outer cylinder. The sulfur deposition at the cylinders was almost not 
observed. 
During the experiment with cylinders in contact with the liquid, the 
biofilm covered cylinders only, and the digester itself was clean 
(Fig. 4C). Fig. 5 shows the view of the cylinders from the underside that 
was in contact with the liquid. The structure of the biofilm was visually 
similar to the biofilm on the wall in the second experiment. The results 
were compared with simulation results and are discussed in Section 3.3. 
2.5. Simulation of biogas flow pattern in the headspace 
2.5.1. Oxygen flow 
Based on the simulation results, oxygen was in all three experiments 
spun at the point of oxygen entry after the first contact with biogas 
(Fig. 6). After entering the reactor, oxygen was immediately carried to 
the biogas outlet. Some oxygen was washed out from the reactor with 
biogas, explaining the oxygen presence (0.2 % vol.) in the biogas. The 
remaining oxygen travelled through the center of the headspace to the 
liquid surface, where it picked up speed again. 
The position of the oxygen dosing point was not ideal. The amount of 
oxygen required for complete H2S oxidation was higher due to the 
washout from the reactor, so the cost of the required oxygen would in­
crease at full-scale. In literature, the stochiometric ratio O2/S2−required 
for complete desulfurization varies among different studies (E.g. 0.5 
[11], 1 – 1.4 [9], 1 [16], or 5.5 [18]. Based on the simulation results, 
when the oxygen is used for desulfurization only, the difference might be 
caused by the position of the dosing point and the subsequent ratio 
between oxygen available to sulfide oxidizing bacteria and oxygen 
drained from the reactor with biogas. However, the evaluation is 
impossible since there is no precise information about the position of the 
dosing point and geometry of the headspace in previously published 
papers. 
2.5.2. The flow of a biogas/oxygen mixture 
In the experiment with empty headspace, the biogas coming from the 
liquid was carried to the walls by centrifugal force together with oxygen 
(Fig. 6A). The gas mixture was evenly distributed throughout the 
headspace. The conditions for sulfide oxidizing bacteria were not 
significantly prioritized at specific places; therefore, the biofilm covered 
the outer wall of the whole headspace. 
In the experiment with cylinders suspended 3 cm above the liquid 
(Exp.2) (6B), the mixture under the cylinders behaved similarly to the 
experiment with empty headspace. Once the mixture reached the cyl­
inders, the mixture flowed to the ceiling and continued to the gaps be­
tween the cylinders. The mixture flowed rapidly from top to bottom 
between the cylinders and returned to the liquid down the center 
(Fig. 7A). Assuming only the z-component of the velocity describing the 
vertical speed of the mixture (Fig. 8), the mixture flowed between the 
cylinders only in a downward direction, shortening the residence time 
between the gaps. The sulfur deposition was observed mainly at the 
reactor’s wall under the cylinders, which was most likely caused by this 
mixture circulation, limited residence time between the cylinders and 
the highest concentration of H2S evolving from the liquid and pushed to 
the wall by centrifugal force. 
In the experiment with cylinders in direct contact with liquid (Exp. 
3), the gas mixture could not be directly pushed to the walls since the 
cylinders interrupted the flow (6C). The mixture flowed from the center 
from one gap to another. It reached the reactor’s wall at the end 
(Fig. 7B). The residence time of the mixture between the cylinders could 
have caused all oxygen was entirely consumed, resulting in no oxidation 
possibility in the gap between the last cylinder and the wall. Assuming 
only the z-component of the velocity, the vertical speed decreased twice 
compared to the experiment with cylinders suspended 3 cm above the 
liquid. Fig. 8 proves that the mixture flowed up and down from one gap 
to another. In the experiment with cylinders in direct contact with 
liquid, the biofilm growth was apparently prioritized between the cyl­
inders, which correlates to the experimental results (Figs. 4 and 5). The 
simulation results correlate with the observed sulfur deposition in the 
reactor in all three experiments.

2.6. Implications for reactor design 
According to the results of the mathematical simulation, the head­
space geometry had a crucial effect on sulfur deposition position and 
oxygen requirements. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time 
the complex headspace geometry effect on microaeration was evaluated. 
Adding the cylinders into the headspace had no adverse effect on 
microaeration efficiency; only the biofilm position was affected. From 
the technological point of view, the worst scenario was the empty 
headspace, where all the walls and structures in the headspace were 
completely covered with sulfur-driven biofilm and could be degraded by 
corrosion. On the other hand, when the cylinders were in direct contact 
with liquid, the microaeration efficiency was not affected, and the di­
gester’s wall was efficiently protected. 
The CFD model developed can be used in every bioreactor modelling 
where the gas is evolved into the headspace from rotating liquid. Given 
that we used an artificial substrate, the rate of biogas emerging from the 
liquid to the gas phase was constant. If biogas production is diverse, it is 
necessary to consider that this rate may influence the mixing patterns in 
headspace and conduct scenario analyses where several biogas flow 
rates are investigated for a specific reactor. 
Installing the baffles into the fermenter will increase investment 
costs compared to classic microaeration, especially when the fermenter 
has already been built. On the other hand, the baffles installed will in­
crease the technology’s lifetime and help to remove sulfur biofilm 
effectively during the cleaning period. Compared to investing in the new 
ex-situ desulphurization, the costs will be many times lower, and no 
additional area will be required. The final financial savings will depend 
on the structure of the existing or newly installed fermenter, the material 
used and the shape of the installation and need to be evaluated in 
dedicated full-scale experiments. 
2.7. Further research 
In the research, an artificial substrate was used to achieve the same 
steady state in all experiments. There is a presumption that results from 
biofilm growth would be similar when the industrial substrate was used 
since the substrate for bacteria is not related to the composition of the 
liquid but H2S presence in biogas. However, this needs to be confirmed. 
In this study, sophisticated and accurate methods for online H2S and 
biogas monitoring were used, which allowed obtaining strong dataset 
about the behavior of the gases in the experiments. On the other hand, 
detailed sulfur analyses of the biofilm were not done due to the lack of 
biological material (dried biofilm) for these analyses. Results from the 
biofilm composition and the microbial abundance in each experiment 
would support the CFD model results. 
The model presented in this study showed the ability to describe gas 
flow in different headspace configurations only by changing the geom­
etry of the headspace in the model. The next step of the research would 
be adding biological processes into the model and simulating the biofilm 
growth and the H2S/oxygen consumption in space. Such simulation

requires high computational complexity [19]. Adding a biological pro­
cess to the model could also provide assurance that there will be no 
development of SOB on undesirable surfaces in the long term. In this 
study, we terminated all experiments only when, for several weeks, 
there was no visual evidence of culture development. Simulation results 
also suggested that there was no biological activity on the reactor walls 
due to substrate scarcity. However, a long-term simulation would bring 
even greater certainty in fermenter design. 
The mathematical model was developed based on knowledge of fluid 
flow. Validation of the model involved comparing the simulation results 
with experimental results, where gas flow, and consequently the 
accessibility of the substrate to bacteria, corresponded to actual in­
creases in biofilm observed in the experiments. In the next phase of the 
research, experiments, including simulations, should be replicated in a 
full-scale situation. 
3. Conclusions 
The CFD model developed in this study described the flow of the 
gases above the rotating liquid surface in anaerobic digesters with 
different reactor headspace configurations. The model supported by 
experimental data explained the effect of headspace geometry on biogas 
and oxygen flow patterns, microaeration efficiency, and the sulfur 
deposition in the headspace. We also showed that when internal baffles 
placed in the headspace disturbed biogas flow, the position of biofilm 
growth was altered. The fact that biogas rotated in the headspace 
directly influenced which surfaces were in contact with both H2S and 
oxygen and hence defined where biofilm developed. Finally, the amount 
of oxygen required for efficient desulfurization was shown to depend on 
the position of the oxygen dosing point. Bioreactor designers can use 
these findings to design headspace geometry so biofilm will form on 
predefined surfaces while protecting the reactor’s walls from biofilm- 
induced corrosion. The research hypothesis that the headspace geome­
try modification can influence oxygen consumption, biogas flow and 
subsequent sulfur deposition in the headspace was confirmed.
